segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One Sabbath, when he went into the house of one of the leaders of the Pharisees to eat bread, they were watching him closely.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there in front of him was a man who had dropsy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus responded by asking the experts in the law and the Pharisees,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they kept silent. So he took hold of the man, cured him, and sent him away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If one of you has a son or an ox that falls into a well, will you not immediately pull him out on the Sabbath day?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were not able to give an answer to this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Noticing how those who had been invited were choosing the places of honor, he told them a parable, saying to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not recline in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited by him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the one who invited both you and him will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then in shame you will begin to take the last place.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he will say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have honor in the presence of all who are reclining at table with you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also said to the one who had invited him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, in case they also invite you in return and you are repaid.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and you will be blessed, because they have no means to repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When one of those reclining at table with him heard this, he said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man was giving a great dinner, and he invited many people.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: At the hour of the dinner he sent his slave to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, because everything is now ready.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But they all alike began to excuse themselves. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Another said, ‘I have bought five pairs of oxen, and I am on my way to try them out. Please have me excused.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and for that reason I cannot come.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The slave came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his slave, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in here the poor and the crippled and the blind and the lame.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the slave said, ‘Master, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the master said to the slave, ‘Go out to the roads and hedgerows and compel them to come in, so that my house may be filled.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I tell you, none of those men who were invited will taste my dinner.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Large crowds were traveling with him, and he turned and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and yes, even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For which of you, wanting to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost, to see whether he has enough to complete it?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it will begin to mock him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or what king, going out to engage another king in war, will not first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet the one coming against him with twenty thousand?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if he is not, while the other is still far away he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way, then, anyone among you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Salt, then, is good; but if even salt becomes tasteless, with what will it be seasoned?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile; people throw it out. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

notes.note: “To eat bread” is a Semitic idiom for having a meal, not a description of the menu. The literal wording is kept because the guest's exclamation in verse 15 uses the same phrase for the feast in the kingdom of God.

Dropsy is the older name for edema, a visible swelling of the body caused by retained fluid. It is a symptom of serious underlying illness and not a disease in itself. The Greek term is a standard medical word of the period and occurs only here in the New Testament.

The word names men learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with the scribes. “Lawyer,” kept by the KJV, ESV and NRSV, suggests to a modern reader an attorney who represents clients in court. The NIV and several other recent versions also use “expert in the law.”

Manuscripts differ here: some read “a donkey or an ox,” and a few read “a sheep.” “Son” has strong early support and is the harder reading, since copyists would more readily change it to an animal to match “ox” than the reverse. Most modern editions and translations read “son” or “child.”

At formal meals guests reclined on couches arranged around the table, and the positions were ranked, with the places nearest the host carrying the most prestige. The Greek word means literally the “first reclining place.” The verbs in verses 8, 10 and 15 are accordingly translated “recline,” where older versions have “sit.”

The Greek word ordinarily means a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Most English versions since the KJV have “servant,” which softens the social reality a first-century reader would have assumed. The NRSV and some other recent versions also have “slave” here.

The verb covers both physical force and strong insistence. Here, where a single slave is sent to strangers who would not expect to be invited to such a meal, most interpreters understand urgent persuasion that will not take a polite refusal, and some versions translate “urge” or “make.” The verse was later cited to justify religious coercion, a use the context does not support.

The “you” is plural in Greek, although the master in the story is speaking to a single slave. Either the master is pictured as addressing his household more broadly, or Jesus here steps out of the parable and speaks directly to his fellow guests, so that “my dinner” becomes his own. The translation keeps the sentence inside the master's speech, as most versions do, but the second reading is widely held.

In Semitic idiom, “love” and “hate” set side by side can express preference, not emotion: to “hate” one thing is to rank it decisively below another (compare Genesis 29:30–31 and Deuteronomy 21:15). The parallel saying in Matthew 10:37 speaks of loving family “more than me.” The strong word is kept because Luke chose it, and softening it would blunt the saying.

notes.traditional: have lost his savour; has lost its taste
notes.note: The verb elsewhere means “to make foolish” (as in Romans 1:22), and its use of salt here and in Matthew 5:13 is unusual; some scholars suspect a wordplay in an underlying Aramaic saying. Pure salt does not lose its saltiness, and the image is often explained by the impure salt of the region, from which the sodium chloride could leach out and leave a useless residue.

candidates.reason: Occurs across the Gospels, Acts and the letters, and translators divide between “slave,” “servant” and “bondservant,” so one decision is needed for parables and for self-designations like “slave of Christ.”
Usually “glory,” but here plainly social honor; the line between “glory,” “honor” and “praise” needs fixing across the New Testament.
Recurs in the Sabbath controversies and in Paul, where versions vary between “lawful,” “permitted” and “allowed.”
The family of reclining verbs (ἀνάκειμαι, κατακλίνω, ἀναπίπτω, συνανάκειμαι) is rendered “sit,” “sit at table” or “recline” by different versions and should be uniform across the Gospels.
When used of a human slave-owner or as a form of address within parables, the choice between “master,” “lord” and “sir” should be consistent, especially where the parable figure shades into Jesus.
